# Principles of medical law and ethics

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Preoperative and postoperative care > Principles of medical law and ethics*

[Original Article Link](/library/DO01uT)

---

## Summary

Best medical practice is founded upon the ethical principles that guide <u>health care providers</u> who care for patients or perform research. The <u>core ethical principles</u> of medicine are <u>autonomy</u>, <u>beneficence</u>, <u>nonmaleficence</u>, and <u>justice</u>. Medical research is also subject to <u>core ethical principles</u> and to specific guidelines and processes to ensure that research in <u>vulnerable populations</u> (e.g., pregnant individuals, children) is conducted ethically. Many laws govern a wide variety of medical situations. A small selection of laws applicable in the United States is described in this overview article, while several other laws are detailed in more specific articles. Local laws can vary significantly. Clinicians must be familiar with the laws that govern practice in their region.




For more specific ethics and laws, see “<u>Capacity, competence, and consent</u>,” “<u>Ethics of communicating medical information</u>,” “<u>Medical professionalism and codes of conduct</u>,” and “<u>Death</u>.”




For ethical and medicolegal dilemmas, see “<u>Challenging clinical and ethical scenarios</u>.”

## Medical ethics

### Core ethical principles [[1]](/library/j_b_Lw)




#### Overview




* <u>Medical ethics</u> is founded on a set of core principles that are based on respect to patients as individuals.

* Ethical dilemmas arise when respecting one of these principles becomes impossible without compromising another.

* Ethical responsibilities usually align with legal precedence, but the two systems remain distinct.





#### Principles




* Autonomy

* Provide sufficient information for the patient to be able to make their own decisions regarding their care (i.e., <u>informed consent</u>).

* Honor the patient's choices to accept or decline care.

* Beneficence

* Advocate for the patient and act in their best interest (fiduciary relationship).

* May conflict with <u>autonomy</u>

* Nonmaleficence

* Avoid causing injury or suffering to the patient.

* May conflict with <u>beneficence</u>: The balance of risks and benefits must be favorable to the patient.

* Frequently discussed in reference to drugs and surgical procedures

* Justice

* Treat patients fairly and equitably.

* Equity is not the same as equality.





### Obligation to treat




* A clinician is legally obligated to treat a patient when failing to provide treatment would immediately endanger the patient's life. [[2]](/library/B_bzqw)

* This law was established in the <u>Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act</u> (<u>EMTALA</u>).

* Any hospital with an emergency department is required to screen for <u>emergency medical conditions</u> if requested and, if such a condition exists, provide treatment until that condition is stabilized.

* Clinicians are not obliged to treat a patient longitudinally and may end a <u>clinician-patient relationship</u> if they wish. [[3]](/library/dlYoD6)

* The patient or their <u>surrogate</u> must be notified and have the ability (e.g., time, money) to establish care with another clinician.

* The clinician is also obligated to facilitate the transfer of care.





### Principle of proportionality




* Definition

* A bioethical principle stating that an intervention's potential benefits should be proportionately greater than its potential harm or burden [[4]](/library/sgWt9k0)

* Benefit, harm, and burden should be considered not only in terms of patient health, but also holistically in terms of, e.g., costs for the patient, costs for the <u>health care system</u> as a whole, and the safety of providers and other patients.

* Aim: to minimize patient harm proportionately to maximizing treatment efficiency

* Examples

* Using <u>physical restraints</u> if a patient poses a threat to themselves or others.

* Reassessment of resource allocation during a health crisis when providing maximum benefit to select patients would overburden the system as a whole.

## Research ethics

### Role of institutional review boards




* Definition: An institutional review board (<u>IRB</u>) is a committee that reviews designs of studies involving humans to ensure participant safety, participant <u>confidentiality</u>, and compliance with <u>medical ethics</u>.

* <u>IRB</u> composition [[5]](/library/VyXGV00)[[6]](/library/sSWtaO0)

* The composition of an <u>IRB</u> can vary across institutions but it should include at least five members with at least one scientist and one non-scientist.

* <u>IRBs</u> that review studies conducted on <u>vulnerable populations</u> should include representatives of the corresponding populations.

* <u>IRB</u> approval [[7]](/library/GSWBaO0)

* For most forms of <u>primary research</u> involving human subjects, an <u>IRB</u> should review and approve the study proposal and <u>informed consent</u> protocols before the research activity is started.

* Any amendment to an approved research protocol must be reevaluated and reapproved by the <u>IRB</u> before the research activity can continue.

* Examples of studies that do not require <u>IRB</u> review and approval include:

* Surveys or interviews about products or policies

* Educational tests

* <u>Secondary research</u> involving publicly available nonidentifiable information





### <u>Informed consent</u> for research [[8]](/library/CzbqEw)[[9]](/library/-aWDMP0)[[10]](/library/rSWfaO0)




* Researchers performing a study involving an intervention on or interaction with human subjects should obtain <u>informed consent</u> from potential participants unless an <u>informed consent</u> waiver has been obtained from the <u>institutional review board</u>.

* The process of obtaining <u>informed consent</u> is initiated by performing the following steps with a potential participant:

* Provide sufficient information verbally and in writing (as a part of the <u>informed consent</u> for research form).

* All aspects of the experimental protocol (i.e., the trial design, purpose, and duration of the research)

* Any foreseeable hazards to the participant

* The likelihood of direct benefit to the participant

* All alternative treatment options, if applicable

* Details about the funding and financial incentives for the researchers, including the sources of such funds

* A statement about the <u>confidentiality</u> of collected information and how records identifying the subject will be maintained

* For research involving more than minimal risk, information on whether any compensation or medical treatments are available in case of injury

* Information on whom to contact regarding questions about the trial and participant rights

* A statement that participation is voluntary at all times and that the participant can withdraw at any time without penalty, loss of benefits to which the participant is otherwise entitled, or obligation to explain the decision.

* Facilitate potential participants' understanding of the provided information and clarify potential misunderstandings.

* Therapeutic misconception: an individual participating in research believes that they are receiving individualized medical treatment or care rather than participating in research. [[11]](/library/FSWgYO0)

* Therapeutic misestimation: an individual misjudges the risk or benefit of participating in research. [[12]](/library/8SWOYO0)

* Provide adequate time and opportunity for potential participants to decide whether or not to participate.

* Minimize the possibility of <u>coercion</u> or <u>undue influence</u>.

* Coercion: an overt or implicit threat of harm made to obtain compliance

* Undue influence: the offer of an inappropriate reward to obtain compliance

* The process of obtaining <u>informed consent</u> is formalized by the participant signing an <u>informed consent</u> for research form that has been approved by the responsible research <u>institutional review board</u>.

* The process of obtaining <u>informed consent</u> is not finalized upon formal enrollment and the signing of an <u>informed consent</u> for research form, but instead extends for the entire duration of the trial.





> [!NOTE]
> Study participants should be updated on information relevant to them throughout the duration of the trial or study. Participants have the right to withdraw consent for research at any time.




### Research funding [[13]](/library/HSWKaO0)[[14]](/library/7SW4aO0)




* Before accepting funding for research, the researcher should contractually ensure that the research sponsor cannot influence, delay, or obstruct the publication of the findings.

* Clinicians should not accept any form of compensation for directing patients to participate in research studies.

* The source of funding should be disclosed as a part of the <u>informed consent</u> process and when publishing the research findings.

* A researcher should refuse to accept financial compensation that surpasses the value of their input in the research and doesn't align with the current market rate.





### Compensation for enrolled participants [[9]](/library/-aWDMP0)




* The type and amount of compensation should be determined prior to study enrollment and should be just and fair for all participants.

* Prorated compensation: Participants receive a predetermined compensation for the completion of each trial activity (e.g., visit, procedure) or compensation that scales up with the duration of enrollment.

* Completion-contingent compensation: Participants receive a predetermined compensation for the completion of all trial activities.

* The amount of compensation should be adequate in relation to the risks, time, and inconveniences demanded by study participation, but should not be excessive or tied to conditions that may affect voluntary consent and thereby constitute <u>coercion</u> or <u>undue influence</u>.

* The participant can withdraw at any time without loss of benefits to which the participant is otherwise entitled.

* If a participant experiences <u>adverse events</u> as a result of participation in the study, the participant is eligible for financial support for medical treatment and may be eligible for additional compensation. [[13]](/library/HSWKaO0)





> [!NOTE]
> Offering compensation that is excessive or contingent on completing all trial activities may constitute <u>coercion</u> or <u>undue influence</u>.




### Research in <u>vulnerable populations</u> [[15]](/library/BtXzf-)




* Vulnerable population: a population that has insufficient ability to protect or advocate for their interests

* In addition to the requirement of obtaining <u>informed consent</u> from study participants, special protections exist for <u>vulnerable populations</u> in research.

* The policy on the protection of <u>vulnerable populations</u> is regulated by the <u>Office for Human Research Protection</u> (<u>OHRP</u>).

* Regulatory and ethical checks are enforced to ensure the protection of populations that are at increased risk of harm in clinical trials.

* Applications and proposals must fulfill <u>OHRP</u> requirements in order to receive federal department or agency support.





#### Pregnant individuals and fetuses




* Permitted research: Clinical trials or research studies on pregnant individuals and fetuses must fulfill the following requirements:

* Preclinical studies involving pregnant animals and clinical studies involving nonpregnant individuals have been conducted prior to the study in question.

* Adequate data regarding the potential risks to pregnant individuals and fetuses is available.

* The clinical trial has the potential to directly benefit the pregnant individual and/or their fetus.

* There are no other means of answering the research question, and the research poses minimal risk for the pregnant individual or fetus.

* Requirements 

* The investigators may not have any role in determining the viability of the fetus.

* No incentive may be offered to terminate a <u>pregnancy</u>.

* If the research is only beneficial to the fetus, paternal consent must also be obtained unless the father is unavailable, temporarily incapacitated, or the <u>pregnancy</u> resulted from <u>rape</u> or incest.





#### <u>Neonates</u>




* Permitted research: Clinical trials or research studies on <u>neonates</u> must fulfill the following requirements:

* The research question is crucial and cannot be answered by other means.

* The research provides a direct benefit to the <u>neonate</u> at no additional risk.

* Requirements

* For <u>neonates</u> of uncertain viability, the research must increase the <u>probability</u> of their survival.

* Nonviable <u>neonates</u> may only be involved in research if:

* Vital functions of the <u>neonate</u> are not artificially maintained.

* The heartbeat and respiration of the <u>neonate</u> will not be terminated by the research.

* Legally effective <u>informed consent</u> must be obtained from the parents, guardians, or legally authorized representatives.





#### Children




* Permitted research: clinical trials that pose no greater risk of harm to children than to adults and pose no other ethical reasons for the exclusion of children

* Requirements

* If the intervention being tested poses a greater risk of harm to children than adults, the trial may only be conducted if the research question cannot be answered by any other means and the research has the potential to directly benefit the individual subjects or is likely to provide generalizable knowledge about the condition being studied.

* Investigators must obtain assent from the child as well as <u>informed consent</u> from the parents.





#### Prison inmates




* Permitted research: The research investigates health issues directly related to the prison inmate population.

* Requirements

* The risks associated with the research may not:

* Be greater for prisoners than for nonprison volunteers

* Pose more than minimal risk

* Be an inconvenience to the subjects

* At least one member of the <u>institutional review board</u> (<u>IRB</u>) that reviews the ethical <u>validity</u> of the study should be a prison inmate or a representative.

* None of the nonprisoner members of the <u>IRB</u> may have any affiliation with the prison.

* Any potential advantages offered to the prison inmates through participation in the research may not be so great that they affect the prison inmate's ability to weigh the risks of participation against the benefits.





> [!NOTE]
> In research, special protections exist for <u>vulnerable populations</u>.




### Participant data protection [[16]](/library/tSWXYO0)




* The <u>HIPAA Privacy Rule</u> establishes guidelines for protecting participant data.

* A <u>covered entity</u> may always use or disclose <u>deidentified health information</u> for research.

* If a <u>covered entity</u> wishes to obtain, generate, use, or disclose <u>individually identifiable health information</u> for research, at least one of the following criteria must be met:

* Participant authorization

* Waiver from an <u>IRB</u> or Privacy Board

* Only the health information of deceased individuals is used or disclosed.





### Participant withdrawal from research [[17]](/library/LxXwCZ0)




* A participant can withdraw from a study at any time without penalty, loss of benefits to which the participant is otherwise entitled, or obligation to explain the decision.

* If a participant wishes to terminate their participation in a clinical trial:

* Researchers may enquire if the participant is willing to share their reasons for wishing to withdraw after reemphasizing to the participant that they are under no obligation to explain the decision.

* Researchers may offer participants to opt-in to select components of the trial only.

* Withdrawal from the trial must be documented.

* Already collected data relating to the participant may be kept and analyzed.

* Data collected for research conducted under <u>FDA</u> regulations may not be destroyed or omitted from the analysis.

## Medical laws

* See “<u>Capacity, competence, and consent</u>” for laws related to <u>decision-making capacity</u>, <u>legal competence</u>, and <u>informed consent</u>.

* See “<u>Ethics of communicating medical information</u>” for laws related to disclosure, <u>confidentiality</u>, and <u>reportable conditions</u> (e.g., <u>HIPAA</u>, <u>duty to protect laws</u>).

* See “<u>Medical professionalism and codes of conduct</u>” for laws related to <u>malpractice</u>, <u>clinician impairment</u>, <u>conflicts of interest</u>, and <u>referral of patients</u> (e.g., <u>Stark law</u>).

* See “<u>Death</u>” for laws related to:

* <u>Death</u> determination, e.g., <u>legal death</u> definition, <u>Uniform determination of death act</u>

* <u>Investigation of death</u>, e.g., <u>autopsy</u>, <u>reportable types of death</u>

* <u>Medical assistance in dying</u>

* See “<u>Goals of care</u>” for legal terms related to <u>end-of-life issues</u>, e.g., <u>code status</u>, <u>withdrawal of care</u>, and forms such as <u>MOLST</u>, <u>NEOT</u>, <u>DNR</u>, and <u>DNI</u>

* See “<u>Health care system</u>” for laws related to <u>health insurance funding</u> (e.g., <u>Medicare</u>, <u>Medicaid</u>) and <u>health care access</u> (e.g., <u>EMTALA</u>, Affordable care act).

* See “<u>Transplantation</u>” for laws related to <u>organ donation</u>.

## Involuntary commitment

* Definition: a legal intervention through which an individual who experiences symptoms of a severe mental disorder can be detained in a mental health facility for involuntary treatment or receive such treatment in outpatient settings [[18]](/library/9GXNY-)

* Regulations [[18]](/library/9GXNY-)

* The criteria differ state-by-state but generally include the following components:

* Mental illness

* Grave disability (e.g., inability to self-feed or shelter)

* Danger to self or others

* Need for treatment

* The commitment settings should be the least restrictive option possible.

* Proceedings for commitment are usually initiated by a family member or <u>health care provider</u>.

* Individuals can typically be held for some period of time specified by the state law without a court order given that the admission is medically certified.

## Abortion and stillbirth laws

* <u>Stillbirth</u>: Offering an <u>autopsy</u> of the fetus and <u>placenta</u> is recommended after a confirmed unexplained <u>stillbirth</u>.  [[19]](/library/nVd7EK0)[[20]](/library/LVdwEK0)

* Abortion: Abortion laws vary greatly state-by-state.  [[21]](/library/UZXba9)[[22]](/library/oVd0vK0)[[23]](/library/y2dd460)

* Most states require that parents of minors undergoing an <u>abortion procedure</u> are notified and/or sufficiently informed to provide consent.

* <u>Patient counseling</u> prior to <u>abortion procedures</u> is mandatory in some states.

* Most states allow clinicians to refuse to perform abortions under the condition that patients are referred to another clinician who is skilled and willing to perform abortions.

* Many states only permit abortions under certain conditions: 

* The pregnant individual's life or health is at risk because of the <u>pregnancy</u>.

* The procedure is performed by a licensed physician.

* The fetus is below a certain <u>gestational age</u>.
